march 1826 — born 29 april 1825, father entered as “george pitt d'arcy, bt: major 39th foot” , mother maria , abode chatham. on 8 april 1826 , eight days later, the surgeon of the convict ship england received aboard a detachment of the 39th commanded by " george pitt d'arcy, b. major ". they christened the baby, and then they sailed. the chatham register → documented this is the part of the pedigree that does not need defending, and it turns out to be the best part. the man at the bottom of the english line is not a footnote: he is a peninsular war officer who commanded the 39th regiment in a general action, and the colony's newspapers said so when he died. the ship the convict ship england , 1826 the surgeon superintendent's journal and the ship's record give the voyage almost day by day. the journal has now been identified at the national archives and it is adm 101/26/1 — "medical journal of the england, convict ship, for 18 march to 29 september 1826 by george thomson, surgeon and superintendent " . until 10 september 2026 this archive cited it only as "the surgeon's journal". it names major d'arcy four times. 8 april 1826 "received on board a detachment of the 39th regt. of foot commanded by george pitt d'arcy, b. major , consisting of 39 men (including 2 sergeants and 3 corporals), 6 women and 7 children . victualled on board and found fit for embarkation." two been: thomas baptised 1744, his marriage to catherine cotton in 1769, john baptised five weeks later, thomas buried 1819 aged 75, john buried 1825 aged 55, and john's children in 1801, 1803 and 1808. children before he died. the d'arcys have been brisbane people for a hundred and sixty years. the family arrived in australia as soldiers at parramatta in 1826. within two generations it had become something quieter and more queensland: clerks, a railway man, an insurance manager. this page follows the four generations that made brisbane home. 1829 george lindsay d'arcy · 1829–1901 king's school, then the diggings born at parramatta, christened at st james's, sydney, and schooled at the king's school, parramatta — his obituary calls him one of its oldest scholars. pastoral work, then the california goldfields. he came to queensland in 1863, took a place in the colonial secretary's office and kept it until he died, and married eliza keeling at brisbane on 7 june 1863 — five months after she stepped off the flying cloud at moreton bay. seven children. buried at dutton park. 1864 george pitt d'arcy · 1864–1931 the railway clerk named for the major of the 39th foot, and the first of the line born in brisbane. chief clerk in the queensland railway department. married ida kathleen atkinson at trinity church, fortitude valley, on 10 october 1888. buried at dutton park beside his father. 1892 lindesay atkinson d'arcy · 1892–1936 the one who died young clerk; brisbane central boys' state school. enlisted 13 december 1915 and married ivy miriam sneyd at albion church on 18 march 1916 — then sailed from sydney on hmat a64 demosthenes on 18 may, nine weeks after the wedding. five children. dead at forty-three, leaving a widow with no trade and no pension. 1927 kenneth lindsay first-hand testimony by three people who were there, recorded within days of his death — but testimony about a childhood they did not witness, told to them by the man himself. for his own life after 1955 it is close to a primary record. for his childhood in the 1930s it is his memory, at seventy years' distance, filtered through theirs. both are worth having. they are not the same thing. method → dad used to say to us that he was so against the idea of there being a eulogy at his funeral that he fully intended coming back to haunt the person who dared deliver one. part 1 delivered by his daughter, gayle dad used to say to us that he was so against the idea of there being a eulogy at his funeral that he fully intended coming back to haunt the person who dared deliver one. as dad was not the slightest bit religious or spiritual, this was perhaps something of a puzzling threat. but i hope that, if to his surprise, dad is hearing these words, he will forgive us for wanting to share with you something of his long and successful life. kenneth lindsay d'arcy was born in sandgate on the 17th of august 1927 and was the youngest of 5 children born to ivy and lindsay. growing up in an old queenslander home at clayfield, he played backyard cricket arcy atkinson atkinsone d arcy d'arcey d'arcy darcey darci darcy dorchaidhe lindesay lindsay lindsey murdo murdoch murdock o dorchaidhe sainger sanigaer sanigar sanigear saniger sanigor sanigre sanninger sinagar sinager sinegar singer sinigar siniger sinnegar sinneger sinnigar snayd snead sneed sneid sneyd snyde swanhanger synager synegar

images gallery everything this archive holds as a picture — which is two things, one of them not a document. the shortness of this page is itself a finding. this family produced four soldiers, a gaol governor, a government printer and a church organist across two hundred years. it has left one photograph of one person , and that only because a newspaper printed it when he came home with a medal. that is not unusual and it is worth saying why. photography was expensive until it was not, and the people in this archive are printers, constables, clerks and labourers, not the sort of family that sat for portraits. what survives of them is what a government wrote down. the documents → photograph · printed 18 january 1919 lance-corporal vivian claude sneyd, m.m. and bar a newspaper halftone, head and shoulders, in a peaked cap and tunic. captioned in the paper: “lance-corporal vivian sneyd, 3rd field ambulance, a.i.f., m.m. and bar.” the brisbane courier, saturday 18 january 1919, page 5, under “on honour's roll” as far as this archive knows, the only photograph of anyone in his generation of this family. → illustration · commissioned for this archive, 2026 the crossing a painted triptych under one horizon: a cold english shore with a great house faint on a hill, a stone quay where a three-masted ship is loading, and a flat gold country with a railway line running out of sight. not a document. commissioned illustration, and the house on the hill is faint on purpose. the archive cannot show that this family ever lived in that house. the middle and the right of the lieutenant-colonel d'arcy — and robert d'arcy had been gazetted to exactly that rank six months earlier. george pitt d'arcy is the best-documented d'arcy in this archive and has never had a page. he is also the join on which the whole australian descent hangs: if he is robert d'arcy's son, the line runs from a royal engineer at chatham to a convict ship and queensland. that he was robert's son has been a family tree's assertion and nothing else — until this. salisbury and winchester journal, monday 23 september 1805, page 3 the notice lately, captain george d'arcy, [of] the [—] foot, son [of] lieut. colonel d'arcy, [to] miss ludlam, of guernsey. documented the same london report of 16 september was carried by the hampshire telegraph on the same day. the scan is damaged and the small connecting words are lost — the regiment's number reads only as “tiie foot”. what survives is the structure of an ordinary marriage notice of the period, and the three facts in it: the groom's name and rank, his father's rank, and the bride. why it matters three things at once it is the first record that makes him anyone's son. every other document this archive holds names george pitt d'arcy as a husband, a father, an officer or a passenger. none has ever named his father. this one does — not by name, but by rank. and the rank fits, to the month. robert d'arcy was gazetted lieutenant-colonel on 1 march 1805, vice nepean, six months before this notice was printed. in september 1805 he was a lieut.-colonel of the royal engineers, which is exactly what the notice calls the groom's father. it this archive has spent weeks looking for hannah saniger's baptism, and on two separate days concluded it was missing from every index money could buy. it is not missing. it is spelled sanigor, and that is one of the very few spellings this site's own alias list did not carry. the search index here knows eleven forms of this surname — sainger, sanigar, sanigaer, sinager, sinneger, sinnegar, sinegar, synegar, synager, singer. it did not know sanigor. neither did the variant matching on the subscription site, which returned her marriage and nothing else however the query was phrased. one vowel. and with it, the whole family john saniger's children at berkeley john saniger's children, all baptised at berkeley, all naming him as father: ann sanigar 1798 william saniger 6 september 1801 jno saniger 18 september 1803 hannah sanigor 18 august 1804 the direct line thos saniger 3 july 1808 almost certainly the thomas sinegar who lived a mile from her in bristol it also closes the thomas sinegar question. he and hannah are both baptised at berkeley to john saniger — she in 1804, he on 3 july 1808 — and he spent his life in the bristol parish next to hers, naming a daughter lydia, a places where this family was born and where it died — counted, not asserted. the shape of the list is the shape of the migration. every place named in a birth or death record among the ancestors, with the number of times it appears and the earliest year it appears . each group is ordered by that year rather than by frequency — so the australian list, read from the top, is the migration itself: parramatta in 1829, kempsey in 1838, brisbane from 1856, and then out along the queensland railway to rockhampton, boulia, gympie and toowoomba. the counts are of places, not of spellings. the exported tree writes the same city four ways — brisbane, brisbane, queensland, australia ; brisbane, qld, australia ; and so on — which would split one place into four and make every figure here meaningless. repeated parts are collapsed and state abbreviations expanded before counting. nothing is merged that is not literally the same place, and where a spelling was folded in it is shown treating saniger as a surname that happens to cluster near berkeley. it is the other way round: saniger is a hamlet in berkeley parish, and the name comes off the land. every page here has said the same thing in the same order — a family called saniger, found at berkeley, then at dursley and cam. the order is wrong. the national archives' catalogue describes men who are " of saniger, berkeley ", and farms and lands lying " in saniger and hamfallow ". saniger is a place, and the surname is taken from it. which explains the thing this archive kept noticing and could not account for. it has repeatedly recorded that the name "concentrates in the vale of berkeley", that the spellings are chaotic, and that "of berkeley" looked like a label somebody applied loosely. a toponymic surname does exactly that: it is invented once, in one parish, and everyone who carries it is from there. how surnames are coined → the catalogue entries two centuries of sanigers at saniger reference date entry sneyd a hanley grocer's son who took the king's shilling, sailed for new south wales in 1832, shot a bushranger dead in the blue mountains in 1839, and finished as governor of brisbane gaol. he is the best-documented man in this archive, and until now nobody had written him down. when the archive stripped the sneyds of their invented descent from keele hall, it was braced to lose something. it gained this instead: not a squire but a sergeant of mounted police , and a life that can be traced through the birthplaces of his own children. how the keele descent was broken → hanley to sydney the 4th (king's own) born at hanley, stoke-on-trent, on 15 march 1810 and christened there on 28 april 1811, the son of samuel sneyd, a grocer of hanley , and elizabeth margaret oliver. in 1832 he came to new south wales with the 4th (king's own) regiment of foot — one of the regiments doing convict-guard duty in the colony, the same work that had brought major george pitt d'arcy out six years earlier. this page is wrong, and it is kept here for that reason. everything below was built on the belief that hannah saniger was not born in gloucestershire — a belief that came from a single yes/no tick in the 1841 census. the 1851 census, taken in the same house, states her birthplace outright: berkeley, gloucestershire . the argument on this page is sound and its premise is false. what actually settled it → when the registrar general took in the nonconformist registers in 1837 they were bound, numbered and shelved as rg 4 . they are the registers of people who did not christen their children in the parish church — baptists, presbyterians, wesleyans, moravians, welsh calvinistic methodists — and they are exactly where a bristol working family of the 1810s is most likely to be found. this archive's errand list has said for weeks that there were five bristol chapel registers to read. that was a guess, and it was wrong by a factor of seven. the catalogue holds 36 . twelve of them can contain a birth between 1805 and 1815 — the window for hannah saniger . the other twenty-four cannot, and can now be struck off without opening them. that is the point of doing this before travelling william hartley sneyd was found dead in victoria park, brisbane, on 12 september 1902. the coronial file has been read in full, and it is published here in full, because an archive that suppresses what it finds is not an archive. this page concerns a death by suicide and quotes a coroner's file, including a medical analysis and the sworn evidence of the man's widow. it is set out plainly and without euphemism. if that is not what you came for, the sneyd family page is the place to go instead. he is cristina's three-times-great-grandfather: william hartley sneyd → arthur william hartley sneyd → ivy miriam sneyd → kenneth lindsay d'arcy → ian → cristina. the family tree carried a death date for him and nothing else at all. this is what was behind it. the finding victoria park, 11 september 1902 he left home a little before nine o'clock on the morning of thursday 11 september 1902. he was sixty-four, a contractor by trade, and he had not been able to work for about twelve years because of an injury to his arm. he had had asthma for ten or twelve years, and a bad attack of it two months before. at about ten the next morning two men walking the railway line through victoria park found him lying between two stacks of railway rails, roughly two hundred yards in from gregory terrace. there was a bottle near him. the government analyst found an ounce and a quarter of crude carbolic acid in his stomach. the minimum fatal dose is about an eighth of an ounce. the magisterial inquiry sat at the brisbane police court on 29 september 1902 and entered the cause of death in errands open questions what we got wrong method two origins, no common ancestor the name d'arcy was coined twice over — once in normandy as the name of a place, once in ireland as the name of a colour. anyone searching the name needs to know that before they start. there is no single founding d'arcy family . the name reaches the english-speaking world by two entirely independent routes, and this is a method problem before it is a history. norman — the name of a place d'arcy is french for "of arcy" : a man named for the land he held. the place is usually given as arcy in la manche, normandy ; some accounts point instead to bois-d'arcy in the yvelines, west of paris. a norman de areci appears as a tenant-in-chief in lincolnshire in the reign of william i. by this route the name is territorial . it tells you where a family held land, and nothing whatever about what they were like. gaelic — the name of a colour darcy , characteristically without the apostrophe, is an anglicisation of o dorchaidhe , from dorcha , "dark" — dark-haired, dark-complexioned, or figuratively secretive. it is a nickname name, and there is nothing norman about it at all. the apostrophe is a hint and not a proof. it leans norman, and it was added, dropped and re-added by clerks, priests, recruiting sergeants and shipping agents for four hundred years. our own family is written both ways across its own records — and its most distinctive given name, lindesay , is spelled lindsay in the very next generation. see the spine → the most misused fact in d'arcy genealogy the tribes of galway d'arcys married into a family that already had an archive of its own. this page was wrong for a day, and the brief it contradicted was right. on 9 september 2026 it claimed the founding brief — "the australian d'arcy family that married falco" — had the shape of it wrong, and that the d'arcys had married defranceski while the defranceskis had married falco. that was my error, not the brief's. i read the root person's spouse where i should have read her parents . the tree is unambiguous: ian kenneth d'arcy married giuseppina falco , and their daughter is the person this archive is built outward from. the d'arcys married falco exactly as the brief said. the defranceski marriage is the next one, in the following generation. recorded with the rest → how they join three archives meet at one marriage and two children. all four of those people are living , and none of these archives publishes living people — so the join is described here and not drawn. this archive runs from yorkshire delivered in 2010. two other headlines look damning and say the opposite of what they seem to. this is the archive's worked example of reading evidence rather than skimming it. the brisbane papers have a great deal to say about this family, and the first lesson of them is that a search result is not a source . three of the headlines below would, left as snippets, put a man in the dock who was standing in the witness box. 11 november 1936 the obituary, and a eulogy written seventy-four years later obituary mr. l. a. d'arcy.— the death occurred suddenly yesterday of mr. lindsay atkinson d'arcy, of botany street, clayfield, who for many years had been on the staff of the brisbane office of the union trustee company of australia, ltd. mr. d'arcy, who was aged 44 years, was the only son of the late mr. g. t. d'arcy, of the railway department, and received his education at the old normal school. he served with the australian forces in france during the great war. the late mr. d'arcy is survived by his widow and five children. the funeral will leave the funeral chapel of john hislop and sons, peel street, south brisbane, at 3.30 p.m. to-day, for the toowong cemetery. — the courier-mail (brisbane), wednesday 11 november 1936, p. 23 · nla.news-article37013266 in march 2010 his son kenneth's children stood up and described a father kenneth had lost at the age of nine. nobody involved had seen this obituary. set the two side by side: the eulogy, 2010 the obituary, 1936 "an old queenslander home at clayfield" "of botany street, clayfield" ken "started work as a 15 she is not. read with a correction, 13 september 2026. this reconstitution excluded hannah saniger from all 81 gloucestershire households because the 1841 census ticked her as born outside the county. the 1851 census names her birthplace: berkeley, gloucestershire . the counts and the families below are sound; the conclusion drawn about hannah was not. where she actually came from → this archive's oldest claim is a gloucestershire family. its only link to that family is one line in a queensland death register naming miriam wakefield 's mother as hannah saniger . searching for hannah by name had failed. repeatedly → so instead of searching for her, the county was reconstituted : all 556 saniger records opened one by one, the father and mother read off each baptism, and the children assembled back into the households they came from. 81 families. then ask which of them could be hers. none of them. not one family in gloucestershire has a mother called lydia — the name the tree gives hannah's mother. not one is a john and lydia. there is exactly one hannah baptised in the whole dataset, at stinchcombe in 1730, and only three families are having children at all between 1795 and 1815, when hannah should have been born. searched and empty, comprehensively method what was actually done records opened 556 205 baptisms, 200 marriages, 151 burials baptisms naming a father 196 of 205 — the rest give the child only households assembled 81 38 with two or more children; 43 with one grouped by parish, father's forename arcy atkinson atkinsone d arcy d'arcey d'arcy darcey darci darcy dorchaidhe murdo murdoch murdock o dorchaidhe sainger sanigaer sanigar sanigear saniger sanigor sanigre sanninger sinagar sinager sinegar singer sinigar siniger sinnegar sinneger sinnigar snayd snead sneed sneid sneyd snyde swanhanger synager synegar wakefeild wakefield

its searchers went through the hospitals and base depots of france and england asking men who had been there. the statements are hearsay, contradictory and often wrong. they are also the only surviving voices of the men who were beside him. he was 5050 private arthur hartley sneyd, 9th battalion — a typist from wooloowin, ivy sneyd's younger brother, and so cristina's great-great-uncle. he had joined the battalion in the line on 29 july 1916 , giving up his sergeant's rank to do it. his service → etaples · 3 november 1916 first: killed by a shell his initials are a.h., and his number — 5050. he belonged to b.co. i knew him personally. as i was coming out of the trenches, wounded, at pozieres, pte. r. kent, b.co. told me he had seen sneyd killed by a shell. kent is still with the batt., i think. — pte. p. r. rhead, 4280, c.co arcy atkinson atkinsone d arcy d'arcey d'arcy darcey darci darcy dorchaidhe murdo murdoch murdock o dorchaidhe sainger sanigaer sanigar sanigear saniger sanigor sanigre sanninger sinagar sinager sinegar singer sinigar siniger sinnegar sinneger sinnigar snayd snead sneed sneid sneyd snyde swanhanger synager synegar

governments write down. the women here bore sixty-seven children between them, and one of them gave the most useful evidence on the site. read the rest of this archive and you would think the family was made of men. that is not a fact about the family; it is a fact about what gets recorded . a soldier has an attestation paper, a service record, a casualty form and a medal roll. a printer has a salary in the blue book. a constable has a staff file. a woman who bore nine children and buried four of them has a marriage line and a burial plot. and yet the single most valuable document in this archive is a woman's testimony. when miriam wakefield stood up in the brisbane police court in september 1902 and said " his father's name was samuel sneyd, gaol governor, his mother's name was catherine ", she settled a question four separate research passes had been circling — and she named catherine mulcahy , a cork housemaid dead forty-four years, whom no other record in this archive connects to that family at all. her evidence in full → the eight wives of the direct line, oldest first. the last column is the number of children the tree records — sixty-seven between them . who out the right of it: a quay, a ship, and a flat gold country with a railway line running out of sight. illustration commissioned for this archive, 2026. this is an archive of the d'arcys of brisbane — and of the 13 families they married, who reached queensland out of limerick, monaghan, cork, ayrshire, lanarkshire, somerset, bristol, london and germany. it is not a pedigree. of the 473 people named here, most are somebody's brother or sister and continued nothing. d'arcy was coined twice over, and the two have nothing to do with each other: in normandy as d'arcy , "of arcy", the name of a place; and in ireland as o dorchaidhe , from dorcha , "dark", the name of a complexion. there is no single founding d'arcy family. the work here is to establish which d'arcys are actually connected, and to say plainly where the evidence stops. the document at the centre of it a detachment of thirty men, and a wife in the cabin for as long as this family has had a pedigree, the interesting end of it was every other page on this site rests on paper. the rule → what an ethnicity estimate is, in one sentence. it compares your genome against reference panels of present-day people from various regions and reports which panels it most resembles. it does not find your ancestors. it cannot name one, date one, or confirm a single link in a pedigree — and the further back a claim sits, the less it can say, until at about eight generations it can say nothing at all. the comparison what the tree predicts, against what the swab says the tree's prediction is computed by walking her pedigree and attributing first time. it immediately produced the 1851 census household the archive had twice reported missing, the marriage it had never found, and the stretch of the berkeley register it had called untestable. the measuring was right. the conclusion quietly drawn from it — that a record not reachable here did not exist in reach — was a statement about a budget. what it produced → a free index is not a record office. every one of them is a partial transcript of somebody else's volunteering, and the only honest way to use one is to find out what it holds before you report what it does not. the method is a control test. the test is always the same: run a name that must be there through the same query that returned nothing. if the control comes back empty too, the silence belongs to the index. of the 15 holdings measured here, 7 turned out to be partial, empty or unreachable — and in every one of those cases this archive had already run a search against them and would have reported
